ISIEC chairman, Hon. Mike Ejiogu, disclosed the postponement while interacting with LEADERSHIP, assuring political parties, the electorate and other stakeholders that a new date, timetable and electoral guidelines would be announced within the shortest possible time.
Ejiogu said the decision followed extensive consultations and engagements with critical stakeholders in the electoral process, and called on all stakeholders to sustain their cooperation and understanding.
He explained that the Commission had, on September 18, 2025, issued a 360-day notification for the conduct of the 2026 local government elections in line with Section 7(1) of the Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria, as amended, Imo State Government Law No. 6, Section 16(1), and the Imo State Independent Electoral Commission Establishment Law 2005, as amended.
According to him, the Commission had initially scheduled the elections for September 26, 2026, following the expiration of the two-year tenure of the 27 Local Government Council Chairmen and Councillors who were elected on September 21, 2024, and sworn into office on September 30, 2024.
He said the earlier date generated concerns among critical stakeholders, particularly the Inter-Party Advisory Council (IPAC), with some members approaching the judiciary to seek an extension of the electoral timeline.
In response, ISIEC embarked on constructive engagements with IPAC and other stakeholders, which resulted in the postponement of the September 26 election to November 7, 2026.
Ejiogu said the latest stakeholders’ meeting was convened to provide an opportunity for further consultations, explain the circumstances surrounding the electoral process and obtain informed suggestions from political parties towards determining a new election date.
He described IPAC as a strategic partner in the electoral process, noting that the Commission could not operate in isolation from political parties and other critical stakeholders.
Ejiogu emphasised that ISIEC remained an impartial electoral management body, independent of political party interests, and committed to providing a level playing ground for all registered political parties, their supporters and candidates.
According to him, the Commission’s allegiance remained firmly with the Constitution, the ISIEC Establishment Law and the people of Imo State.
He reassured political parties and candidates that the Commission would guarantee a transparent and credible electoral environment that would allow all qualified candidates to participate freely.
On security, Ejiogu called on political parties, supporters and aspirants to demonstrate political tolerance, shun violence, thuggery, hate speech and other activities capable of undermining democratic stability.
He cautioned against the destruction of opponents’ campaign billboards and posters, as well as inflammatory comments capable of causing a breakdown of law and order.
The ISIEC chairman revealed that the Commission was working in collaboration with security agencies towards establishing the Inter-Agency Consultative Committee on Election Security (ICCES), comprising the Nigeria Police Force, Nigerian Army, Nigerian Navy, Nigerian Air Force, Department of State Services (DSS), Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps (NSCDC) and other relevant security agencies.
He said the security agencies would ensure adequate security before, during and after the elections, and charged political parties to embrace and sign a Peace Accord, stressing that no individual or group would be allowed to undermine the will of the electorate.
Ejiogu reminded political parties of the need to uphold internal democracy by conducting credible and transparent primaries, noting that the Electoral Act 2022 requires ISIEC to observe political party primaries.
He said the emergence of credible candidates through democratic internal processes would strengthen the legitimacy of the forthcoming elections.
He disclosed that the elections would cover 4,758 polling units and 305 wards across the 27 council areas of the state.
Ejiogu urged traditional rulers, presidents-general, religious leaders, women and youth organisations to support the Commission through grassroots sensitisation and mobilisation to encourage massive voter participation and reduce voter apathy.
He described the traditional institution as an important partner in grassroots democratic development, given its influence and position as custodian of the people’s culture and traditions.
Ejiogu reiterated that despite the postponement, ISIEC remained fully committed to discharging its constitutional responsibility of conducting peaceful, transparent and credible local government elections that would produce democratically elected chairmen and councillors across the state.
Reacting, the state chairman of the African Democratic Congress (ADC), Prof. James Okoroma, said the postponement was a gimmick to delay the party.
“Election cannot be postponed indefinitely without a new, gazetted timetable. Shortest possible time is not a date. Candidates have spent money, printed posters, mobilised agents. Indefinite postponement drains opposition parties while the ruling party stays in power through Sole Administrators,” Okoroma said.
“If you postpone three times, you are not preparing an election, you are preparing an excuse. Give us a date, give us a timetable, and let Imo people vote.
“We demand transparency. ISIEC has not given a specific reason for the 7th of November postponement, beyond consultations and constraints.”
